title: Build v0.6 LLM behaviors: provider interface, prompt assembly, replay cache
body:
Puts LLMs on the active-graph substrate without breaking the trust the
substrate built. Every LLM call is two events (llm.requested,
llm.responded) in the log; the parsed structured output is the only
thing the developer's handler touches; the trace, provenance, budgets,
and replay machinery all keep meaning.

New public surface:
- @llm_behavior decorator with 4-arg handler (event, graph, ctx, llm_output)
- LLMProvider protocol; AnthropicProvider as reference; RecordedLLMProvider
  + RecordingLLMProvider for tests
- Pydantic v2 output schemas, validated server-side after parsing
- AssembledPrompt with public build_prompt() for debugging; view
  serialization format locked + snapshot-tested
- replay_llm_cache=True on Runtime.load / runtime.fork pre-populates a
  content-keyed cache from recorded llm.responded events
- Decimal-precise cost budget (max_cost_usd) with conservative pre-call
  estimation; count_tokens roundtrip skipped on cache hit
- Causal chain crosses LLM boundary via provenance.llm_request_event_id

Failures stay first-class graph citizens: behavior.failed payloads gain
an optional `reason` (llm.network_error, llm.rate_limited,
llm.parse_error, llm.schema_violation, llm.fixture_missing,
budget.cost_exhausted). No silent retries; retries become user
behaviors that subscribe to behavior.failed.

replay_strict + LLM behaviors implicitly turns on the cache (verification
must not hit the live API) and raises ReplayDivergenceError pinned to
the offending llm.requested event id when the re-assembled prompt's
hash doesn't match the recorded one. Cache cannot paper over real
drift in prompt construction.

Demo (examples/llm_claim_extraction.py) was written first per CONTRACT
#20: three documents, structured-output claim extraction, a confidence
flag, a relation behavior tagging source docs, a cached fork, and a
causal chain that walks claim -> LLM call -> source doc -> goal.

147 tests passing (72 v0/v0.5 + 75 new); v0/v0.5 snapshots stay
byte-identical.

KNOWN LIMITATION (narrowed, not closed): drift now detected at
prompt-construction time via the prompt-hash check; provider-side
response drift remains best-effort because Anthropic's messages API
has no seed parameter. Revisits with v0.7 multi-provider routing.

title: Build v0.7 tools + Cypher pattern subscriptions
body:
Tools are a first-class primitive — registered via @tool, invoked
through tool.requested / tool.responded event pairs, replayed from a
content-keyed cache. The runtime owns the LLM ↔ tool turn loop; LLM
behaviors declare tools=[...] and receive only the final parsed
output. Reference tools ship: web_fetch (stdlib urllib) and graph_query
(via make_graph_query_tool factory). All tools serve from cache on
replay by default; replay_reinvoke_deterministic=True opts in to
re-invocation.

Pattern subscriptions land as a strict Cypher subset: node + relation
patterns with type and equality props, multi-hop linear chains, WHERE
with AND/NOT and NOT EXISTS, relationship variable binding. Anything
outside the subset (OR, RETURN, variable-length paths, etc.) raises
UnsupportedPatternError pinned to the offending token. Patterns
compile at registration; matches surface via ctx.matches.

activate_after=N schedules a behavior N events later, event-tick model
only (wall-clock is intentionally out of scope). where= is re-checked
at fire time so stale schedules silently skip.

Provenance gains tool_request_event_ids; the causal chain walks both
LLM and tool boundaries. Trace gets [tool.requested], [tool.responded],
[pattern.matched], [behavior.scheduled] lines, and the v0.6 follow-up
prompt_normalized=true marker on [llm.requested]. All v0/v0.5/v0.6
tests pass unchanged.

Demo: examples/diligence_with_tools.py exercises everything end-to-end
— question generation, tool-using research, contradiction critic via
pattern, activate_after nag, save+fork with both caches, causal chain
that crosses every boundary. 247 tests pass (100 new in v0.7).

title: Build v0.8 Postgres + observability + operator CLI
body:
Hardens the boundary between the runtime and the world it has to live
in. The framework stops adding capability and starts being deployable.

Persistence
- PostgresEventStore behind the same EventStore protocol as SQLite
  (BIGSERIAL, TIMESTAMPTZ, JSONB; identical UNIQUE(id, run_id))
- Connection URLs everywhere (sqlite:///, sqlite:////, postgres://)
- Transaction-per-run migration with ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING
  idempotency; failures roll back and don't block other runs
- EventStoreConformance suite reused across InMemory / SQLite /
  Postgres (the Postgres run is gated on ACTIVEGRAPH_TEST_POSTGRES_URL)

Observability
- Structured JSON logging on opt-in configure_logging(); documented
  schema (timestamp, level, run_id, event_id, behavior, tool, model,
  cache_hit, cost_usd, latency_seconds, reason, error_*)
- Metrics protocol: three methods (counter / histogram / gauge),
  NoOpMetrics default, opt-in PrometheusMetrics
- 20 standard metrics with Prometheus-native naming
  (_total / _seconds / _usd); cardinality rule locked: run_id is
  gauge-only, enforced by the conformance test
- Cache hits and failures as separate counters, not tag values, so
  dashboards become one-line rate queries

Runtime introspection
- runtime.status(recent=N) returns a frozen RuntimeStatus snapshot
- State is log-derived so live and CLI-loaded views agree
- No last_error field; errors are events, filter recent_events

CLI (click)
- activegraph {inspect,replay,fork,diff,export-trace,migrate}
- Thin wrapper around library APIs; --json on every subcommand
- Exit codes locked: 0/1/2/3/4/5 for ok/err/usage/notfound/corrupt/diverge

Docs
- docs/operating.md as the operator-facing guide
- examples/operate_a_run.py as the v0.8 contract (built first;
  every other piece designed backward to make it run)
- CONTRACT.md v0.8 addendum (#1–#19)
- README updates: cache-hit-by-default headline in v0.7, tool closure
  pattern callout, deterministic-test rule in Contributing

Backward compatibility absolute: all 247 v0–v0.7 tests pass unchanged;
83 new v0.8 tests; trace printer output byte-identical for non-
LLM / non-tool runs.

title: Build v0.9 pack format + Diligence pack
body:
Pulls packs forward from v1.0 to v0.9, with one production-quality
reference pack shipping in the same milestone. The pack format is
defined by what the first pack needs.

Six locked design revisions, confirmed before any code was written
(CONTRACT v0.9 #1-#26):

  #3 No module-import side effects. Pack-aware decorators
     (activegraph.packs.behavior/llm_behavior/relation_behavior/tool)
     attach metadata to the function but skip the global registry.
     A pack module is safe to import without a runtime.

  #10 Prompt content hash is the replay contract; declared version
     is for humans. TOML frontmatter (tomllib stdlib, no YAML).
     ReplayDivergenceError fires on hash mismatch even when the
     author forgot to bump the version.

  #8 Canonical-strict / lookup-lenient namespacing. Behaviors and
     tools are prefixed (diligence.claim_extractor) in the trace,
     metrics, errors, and replay manifest. Short-name lookup
     resolves when unambiguous; the load-time conflict check makes
     "unambiguous" a load-time invariant.

  #7 Typed settings injection as primary. Behaviors get pack
     settings via parameter type annotation; ctx.settings is the
     untyped fallback for the pack's own settings;
     ctx.pack_settings("name") handles the rare cross-pack case.

  #5 Load-order asymmetric validation (option a). Object schemas
     apply post-load only; pre-load creation is the v0.8 untyped
     behavior. The pack.loaded event is in the log so replay
     enforces the same load order.

  #16/#17 One-shot question generation in v0.9; contradiction
     detector but no resolver. Adaptive generation and resolution
     are v1.0.

What's new:

  - Pack, ObjectType, RelationType, PackPolicy, PackPrompt,
    EmptySettings, PendingApproval — frozen dataclasses with full
    validation at construction.
  - Pack exception hierarchy (PackError root): PackValidationError,
    PackConflictError, PackVersionConflictError, PackSchemaViolation,
    PackSettingsMissingError, PackPromptLoadError.
  - load_prompts_from_dir() — TOML frontmatter parser + sha256:16
    content hash per prompt.
  - discover() / load_by_name() / clear_discovery_cache() — Python
    entry-point discovery under the activegraph.packs group.
  - Runtime.load_pack() — idempotent, pre-mutation conflict detection,
    namespace prefixing, settings injection, schema attachment.
  - Runtime.pending_approvals() / approve() — minimal approval flow
    so PackPolicy.requires_approval has a gate to enforce.
  - Runtime.get_behavior() / get_tool() — short-name resolution with
    AMBIGUOUS sentinel for cross-pack collisions.
  - Context.settings / pack_settings() / propose_object() — three
    settings access forms plus the approval proposal helper.
  - Graph schema validators — opt-in hooks for object/relation type
    validation, attached by load_pack, None by default (backward
    compat).
  - activegraph.packs.diligence — the reference pack: 8 object types,
    6 relation types, 7 behaviors (4 LLM, 3 deterministic / pattern),
    3 pack-scoped tools, 2 policies, 4 prompts with TOML frontmatter,
    DiligenceSettings (Pydantic), and recorded fixtures for three
    companies (Northwind Robotics, Stellar Logistics, Pinecone Bio).
  - examples/diligence_real_run.py — the killer demo. Runs end-to-end
    against fixtures, produces three memos with the contracted
    structure, demonstrates the memo_approval policy, forks with an
    alternative thesis, exports the trace, walks the causal chain.
  - activegraph pack new <name> — scaffolding command. Generates a
    runnable package with pyproject.toml entry-point registration,
    object_types/behaviors/tools/settings stubs, an example prompt
    with TOML frontmatter, a smoke test, and a README.
  - activegraph pack list — enumerates installed packs via the
    activegraph.packs entry point group.
  - docs/pack_authoring.md — the pack authoring guide. Companion to
    the killer demo (the executable spec) and CONTRACT v0.9 (the
    locked decisions).
  - 54 new tests: pack construction, decorator side-effect isolation,
    prompt loading (frontmatter, hash, error paths), pack loading
    (idempotency, version conflict, contributor conflicts,
    pre-mutation guarantee), settings (defaults, required, dict
    coercion, all three access forms), schema validation
    (post-load only, no-pack backward compat), namespace prefixing,
    scaffolding (CLI, generated pack passes its own smoke test),
    Diligence pack integration (verifiable memo bar, prompt hashes
    in pack.loaded, contradiction detection on Stellar, killer demo
    subprocess).

Backward compatibility (CONTRACT v0.9 #21): all 330 v0-v0.8 tests
pass unchanged. No existing API changes shape. Graph.add_object is
unchanged in the no-packs-loaded case. v0.7's diligence example
(examples/diligence_with_tools.py) stays in place per #22.

Python floor raised to 3.11 (tomllib in stdlib, no new YAML
dependency added). pydantic moved from optional [llm] extra to
hard dep — packs need it for both object schemas and settings.

384 passing tests + 9 Postgres-gated skipped.

title: v1.0-rc2: Fix queue_depth regression and add tutorial tests
body:
## Summary

This release addresses findings from the v1.0-rc1 user-test gate, including a latent runtime bug in `_requeue_unfired` that caused false event requeuing on `Runtime.load`, and adds CI tests for tutorial snippets to prevent spec-vs-impl drift.

## Key Changes

### Bug Fixes

- **Fixed `_requeue_unfired` false-positive requeuing (C3)**: The function incorrectly treated "no `behavior.started` references this event" as equivalent to "event was still in queue." Events with zero subscribers are popped-and-discarded with no `behavior.started` emitted, causing them to be falsely requeued. The fix uses `runtime.idle` as the high-water mark—only events emitted after the last drain are requeue candidates. This resolves `queue_depth` reading nonzero on freshly loaded cleanly-drained runs.

- **Fixed `activegraph --version` reporting**: Version was stuck at 0.9.1 through rc1. Updated to 1.0.0rc2 in both `__init__.py` and `pyproject.toml`.

- **Fixed interactive mode collision prompt**: Unrecognized input now re-prompts instead of silently falling through to the suffix branch, preventing accidental file creation from typeahead input.

### New Tests & Documentation

- **Tutorial snippet execution gate** (`tests/test_tutorial_snippets.py`): Subprocess-runs the step 7 fork snippet end-to-end against bundled fixtures, verifying exit 0 and idempotency. Tactical down-payment on v1.1 #2 (spec-vs-impl drift gate for Python doc snippets).

- **`_requeue_unfired` regression tests** (`tests/test_requeue_unfired.py`): Locks the C3 regression vector with tests verifying `queue_depth == 0` on loaded cleanly-drained runs and that crash-recovery still works when no drain marker exists.

- **PyPI publish workflow** (`.github/workflows/publish.yml`): Tag-push trigger on `v*` builds sdist + wheel and publishes via PyPI trusted publishing (OIDC-based, no long-lived secrets).

- **Publishing guide** (`docs/about/publishing.md`): Documents the release workflow, trusted publishing setup, verification steps, and rollback procedures.

### Documentation Updates

- **Tutorial step 3 prose**: Clarifies the distinction between the provider layer (produces responses) and the runtime's replay cache layer (records and replays `llm.responded` events under strict-replay or in-process fork).

- **Tutorial step 7 fork snippet**: Updated to use `RecordedDiligenceProvider(companies=THREE_COMPANIES)` explicitly, matching the parent run's provider. Includes cleanup-on-collision branch for re-runnable execution.

- **Quickstart output prose**: Corrected explanation of LLM calls to reflect fixture provider behavior rather than cache hits, with clarification of the two-layer architecture.

- **CONTRACT.md**: Added v1.0 #C8 (PyPI publishing externally owned) and expanded v1.1 #2 scope to cover executable Python snippets in docs.

## Implementation Details

The `_requeue_unfired` fix scans the event log for the last `runtime.idle` or `runtime.budget_exhausted` event. Events at or before that marker have been processed; only events after are candidates for requeue. The function falls back to full-log scanning if no drain marker exists (preserving crash-recovery for pre-drain crashes). `runtime.budget_exhausted` is explicitly excluded as a drain marker to avoid breaking budget-bounded pause-and-resume workflows.

Version bumped to 1.0.0rc2 (PEP 440 normalized form) with corresponding tag `v1.0-rc2`.

title: Fix docs build by installing mkdocstrings plugin
body:
## Summary

Fixes a silent documentation build failure where the `mkdocstrings` plugin was declared in `mkdocs.yml` but never installed by the CI workflow. This caused every docs build to fail since the doc-site phase, though the failure went unnoticed until the deploy-verification gate ran post-rc3-merge.

## Changes

- **Added `docs` optional dependency extra to `pyproject.toml`** that includes `mkdocs`, `mkdocs-material`, and `mkdocstrings[python]`. This centralizes documentation build dependencies in one place.

- **Updated `.github/workflows/docs.yml`** to install from the new `docs` extra (`pip install -e ".[docs]"`) instead of hardcoding the dependency list. This prevents future drift between the workflow install step and `mkdocs.yml` configuration.

## Implementation Details

The root cause was a configuration drift: `mkdocs.yml` declared the `mkdocstrings` plugin (added during the doc-site phase), but `.github/workflows/docs.yml` only hardcoded `pip install mkdocs mkdocs-material`. Every docs build silently failed with "plugin not installed" but the artifact upload step never ran, masking the issue.

By moving the dependency list to `pyproject.toml` and having the workflow install from that extra, the pattern now matches all other workflows (`types.yml`, `docstrings.yml`, `wheel-completeness.yml`, `deploy-verification.yml`), ensuring single-source-of-truth for documentation dependencies.

The `pymdownx.*` markdown extensions referenced in `mkdocs.yml` are covered transitively by `mkdocs-material`, so no additional extensions needed to be added.

title: v1.0.2: Provider-aware default model and cross-provider validation
body:
## Summary

This patch release addresses a critical finding from the second external user-test: `@llm_behavior` decorators without an explicit `model=` argument silently inherited a hardcoded Anthropic-family default (`"claude-sonnet-4-5"`), causing HTTP 404 errors when the runtime was configured with `OpenAIProvider`. The error message provided no hint of the cross-provider mismatch.

v1.0.2 makes model defaults provider-aware and validates explicit model names at registration time, catching misconfigurations before the first network call.

## Key Changes

### Protocol Widening (Additive, Backward Compatible)
- **`LLMProvider.default_model`** attribute: Each provider declares its default model
  - `AnthropicProvider.default_model = "claude-sonnet-4-5"`
  - `OpenAIProvider.default_model = "gpt-4o-mini"`
- **`LLMProvider.recognizes_model(name: str) -> bool`** method: Returns True for model names the provider serves
  - `AnthropicProvider` recognizes `claude-*` prefixes
  - `OpenAIProvider` recognizes `gpt-*`, `o1-*`, `o3-*`, `o4-*` prefixes

### Behavior Changes
- **`@llm_behavior(model=...)`** default changed from `"claude-sonnet-4-5"` to `None`
  - Omitting `model=` now resolves to the configured provider's `default_model` at registration time
  - Explicit `model="..."` strings continue to work unchanged
- **`LLMBehavior.model`** field type changed from `str` to `Optional[str]`
  - Pickled v1.0.1 instances deserialize cleanly
  - Freshly-decorated v1.0.2 behaviors carry `None` until runtime resolution

### Registration-Time Validation
- When a behavior pins `model=` explicitly and the configured provider doesn't recognize it, the runtime checks if a *different* shipped provider claims the name
- If exactly one other shipped provider recognizes the name, raises `InvalidRuntimeConfiguration` with structured error naming both providers and the way to fix it
- **Permissive by default**: Unknown names (custom deployments, fine-tunes like `ft:gpt-4o-mini:org::id`) pass silently—only *recognized* cross-provider mismatches fire

### Backward Compatibility
- Custom providers that pre-date v1.0.2 and don't implement `default_model` or `recognizes_model` continue working
- Runtime uses `getattr(provider, "default_model", None)` and `getattr(provider, "recognizes_model", lambda _: False)` for soft requirements
- `LLMBehavior.build_prompt(event, graph)` keeps its v0.6 #20 contract: callable without a Runtime, falls back to `"claude-sonnet-4-5"` for inspection-time hash stability when `model` is `None`

## Implementation Details

- **`_resolve_and_validate_llm_models(source, provider)`** in `runtime.py`: Stamps provider defaults onto behaviors with `model=None` and validates explicit model names against cross-provider mismatches at `Runtime._ensure_registry()` time
- **`_which_shipped_provider_claims(name, exclude)`**: Helper that checks `AnthropicProvider` and `OpenAIProvider` to identify which shipped provider (if any) recognizes a model name
- Updated `examples/babyagi.py` to drop per-provider model tables—behaviors now inherit the correct default from the configured provider
- Documentation updated in `docs/reference/llm-providers.md` with "Default model resolution" and "Cross-provider model-name validation" sections

title: v1.0.2.post1: validation boundary corrected to match CONTRACT v1.0.2 #1
body:
## Summary

Post-release fix to v1.0.2 (PR #15). The CONTRACT amendment that landed in v1.0.2 promised registration-time validation; an external spot-check found the implementation was firing the validation lazily at first `run_goal()` / `run_until_idle()` / `run_until()` via `_ensure_registry()`. The validation logic and the error message were correct — the boundary was wrong.

This post-release moves the validation to **both binding moments** so cross-provider model mismatches fail fast at setup time:

1. **`Runtime(graph, llm_provider=...)` construction** — runs the bulk validation pass against whatever is already registered (global registry, explicit `behaviors=[...]`, or pack-loaded).
2. **`register()` / `@llm_behavior` decoration** — when one or more Runtimes are alive, the freshly-registered behavior is checked against each live Runtime's provider via a `weakref.WeakSet`. The WeakSet auto-cleans on GC; no `Runtime.close()` is added.

The lazy `_ensure_registry()` path stays in place as a defensive double-check for code paths that bypass both binding moments (currently: pack behaviors registered after Runtime construction via `load_pack`). Pack-load-time validation is filed as a v1.1 candidate if friction surfaces.

## Why a post-release, not v1.0.3

The error message is byte-identical to v1.0.2. What changed is *when* it fires — at `Runtime(...)` construction or at `@llm_behavior` / `register()` time, instead of at first `run_goal()`. That's a correction to v1.0.2's broken contract promise, not a new release with new capability. PEP 440 `.post1` is the right shape.

The four v1.0.3 / v1.1 findings (output_schema dict acceptance, silent `behavior.failed` UX, etc.) stay scheduled for their target release. Not folded in.

## Commit shape (four commits)

1. **`fef5051` — CONTRACT clarification.** v1.0.2 #1 (b) wording names both binding moments and the WeakSet implementation pattern. Locked decision first, code second.
2. **`855ec1e` — Implementation.** New module `activegraph/runtime/_live.py` owns the WeakSet + `track_runtime` + the single-behavior cross-provider validator. Both binding moments invoke the same check; the bulk function in `runtime.py` delegates per-behavior. `Runtime.__init__` runs validation *before* self-tracking so failed constructions stay out of the live-set (matters for pytest exception-traceback strong-refs).
3. **`9dace04` — Tests.** Seven new scenarios in `tests/test_llm_default_model.py`:

   - README quickstart pattern works for the matching case
   - decorator without `model=` after Runtime construction stamps the default
   - two Runtimes with different providers both participate in validation
   - failed-construction Runtime doesn't leak into the live-set
   - fork() inherits parent provider, validation is a no-op on the happy path
   - `tests/conftest.py` clears the live-set in the autouse isolation fixture (the WeakSet auto-cleans on GC in production; only test isolation needs the explicit clear).
4. **`e22df5d` — Release.** `1.0.2` → `1.0.2.post1` in `pyproject.toml` and `activegraph/__init__.py`. CHANGELOG entry under `v1.0.2.post1` framed as boundary correction. Three error snapshots rebaselined for the new version string.

title: Adoption-surface gap: OpenTelemetry implementation of the Metrics protocol
body:
## Problem statement

Teams adopting activegraph into production observability stacks need to ship its runtime metrics (events emitted, behavior dispatch, LLM cache hits, cost histograms, queue depth) to the backends they already operate. Today the framework ships two `Metrics` implementations (`NoOpMetrics`, `PrometheusMetrics`) and positions Prometheus as the canonical operator path. The standard metric list itself (`activegraph_*` snake_case names, units in suffixes per `_seconds` / `_usd` / `_total`, fixed tag schemas in `METRIC_NAMES`) is already shaped along OpenTelemetry conventions, but no OTel-compatible implementation ships in the framework.

The outcome a team currently faces: if they run Honeycomb, Phoenix (Arize), Langfuse, Datadog, Grafana Cloud OTLP, or any other OTLP-native backend, they have to either stand up Prometheus alongside their existing telemetry pipeline or hand-roll a `Metrics` adapter against the OTel SDK. The OTel SDK is the de-facto vendor-portable telemetry layer in Python today; the gap is meaningful for adoption.

## Current workaround

Implement the `Metrics` Protocol against the OTel SDK in user code:

```python
from opentelemetry.metrics import get_meter

class _OTelMetrics:
    def __init__(self):
        self._meter = get_meter("activegraph")
        # Per-(name, sorted-tag-keys) instrument cache; OTel disallows
        # re-registering instruments with diverging types or attribute sets.
        self._instruments: dict[tuple, object] = {}

    def counter(self, name, tags, value=1.0):
        # lazy-create Counter, record .add(value, attributes=tags)
        ...

    def histogram(self, name, tags, value):
        # lazy-create Histogram, record .record(value, attributes=tags)
        ...

    def gauge(self, name, tags, value):
        # OTel splits synchronous UpDownCounter from asynchronous
        # ObservableGauge. The Protocol's gauge() is synchronous
        # point-in-time .set, so the wrapper has to track the last value
        # per key and compute deltas, or move to an observable model.
        ...
```

This works, but every adopter rebuilds the same wrapper. The OTel gauge mapping in particular is non-obvious, and the CONTRACT v0.8 #C4 cardinality rule (`run_id` gauge-only, never on counters or histograms) has to be re-enforced in user code rather than once in the framework.

## Proposed solution

An `OTelMetrics` (or `OpenTelemetryMetrics`) implementation alongside `NoOpMetrics` and `PrometheusMetrics`, in the same shape:

- New module at `activegraph/observability/otel.py` with a single class.
- Lazy import of `opentelemetry-api` and `opentelemetry-sdk` via the same `MissingOptionalDependency(package=..., feature=..., extras=...)` pattern used by `PrometheusMetrics`.
- New extra: `pip install 'activegraph[opentelemetry]'`.
- Instruments cached by `(name, sorted-tag-keys)`, matching the `PrometheusMetrics` caching pattern.
- Counters map to OTel `Counter`; histograms map to OTel `Histogram`; gauges map to OTel `UpDownCounter` (or `ObservableGauge`, see open questions).
- Standard metric names from `METRIC_NAMES` ship through OTel as-is. Resource attributes such as `service.name=activegraph` set via the SDK's MeterProvider rather than per-call tags.

Shape stays parallel to `PrometheusMetrics`. The `validate_cardinality_rule()` import-time hook continues to hold for the metric list; an OTel implementation inherits the discipline.

## Open questions

1. Gauge mapping. OTel splits synchronous `UpDownCounter` from asynchronous `ObservableGauge` (callback-driven). The framework's `gauge()` Protocol method is synchronous (point-in-time `set`). `UpDownCounter` exposes `.add(delta)` rather than `.set(value)`, so emulating `set` requires tracking the last value per key and computing the delta. Locking the choice (synchronous emulation vs. moving the standard gauges to an observable model) shapes the implementation and the test contract.

2. Histogram bucket strategy. Prometheus defaults to its own linear buckets. OTel SDK defaults to exponential buckets via the View API. For `activegraph_llm_tokens_in`, `activegraph_llm_tokens_out`, `activegraph_llm_cost_usd`, and `activegraph_behaviors_duration_seconds`, locking the bucket strategy (explicit defaults shipped with the implementation? SDK default? leave to the operator's MeterProvider?) determines whether OTel and Prometheus dashboards show comparable distributions without per-operator tuning.

3. Scope: metrics only, or trace export too? The framework already emits a structured event log (`activegraph/trace/`). A parallel OTel path could map events to OTel spans (one span per behavior invocation, `behavior.failed` as a span event, `llm.requested` / `llm.responded` as nested spans). This is materially bigger; it is a tracing surface rather than a metrics one. Surfacing it here so it can be scoped in or out explicitly rather than left ambiguous.

4. Naming. `OTelMetrics` vs `OpenTelemetryMetrics`. `PrometheusMetrics` set the precedent toward the full word; the file would then be `otel.py` (parallel to `prometheus.py`) but the class `OpenTelemetryMetrics`. Cosmetic, but the project tends to lock these decisions explicitly.

5. Conformance test shape. The `validate_cardinality_rule()` pattern (dataclass-based `METRIC_NAMES` table, validated at import time) suggests an analogous conformance test for the OTel path: drive the runtime through a recorded fixture, collect via OTel SDK's `InMemoryMetricReader`, and assert every `METRIC_NAMES` entry is produced when its source event fires. Confirming the test shape before implementation begins shortens the review loop.

title: feat(store): add FalkorDBEventStore backend (v1.1 STORE-FALKORDB)
body:
## Summary

Phase 1 of the FalkorDB integration: a third `EventStore` implementation
alongside SQLite and Postgres, opt-in via `pip install activegraph[falkordb]`.

[FalkorDB](https://www.falkordb.com/) is a Redis-module property graph
database with OpenCypher. The event log is modelled as a small graph
(`(:Run)-[:HAS_EVENT]->(:Event)`) so operators who pick FalkorDB can
ad-hoc-query the audit trail in Cypher — the same DSL the framework
already uses for behavior subscriptions.

Closes the 2026-05 user request to add FalkorDB support; filed in
`v1.1-plan.md` as `STORE-FALKORDB`.

## Changes

- **`activegraph/store/falkordb.py`** — new module. Full `EventStore`
  protocol (`append` / `iter_events` / `get_event` / `count` /
  `truncate_after` / `close`) + v0.5 run helpers
  (`get_run`/`upsert_run`) + graph-level helpers (`list_runs`,
  `most_recent_run_id`, `fork_run`). Three target shapes accepted (URL
  string, `falkordb.FalkorDB` client, `falkordb.Graph` instance),
  mirroring `PostgresEventStore`.
- **`activegraph/store/url.py`** — register `falkor://` and
  `falkordb://` schemes; `parse_store_url` returns
  `falkordb_graph`; `open_store` dispatches lazily.
- **`activegraph/store/__init__.py`** — lazy export of
  `FalkorDBEventStore` so importing `activegraph.store` does not
  require the optional dep.
- **`pyproject.toml`** — new `[falkordb]` extra (`falkordb>=1.0`);
  added to `[all]` and `[dev]`; new `falkordb` pytest marker.
- **Tests**:
  - `tests/test_falkordb_store.py` — `EventStoreConformance` subclass
    gated on `ACTIVEGRAPH_TEST_FALKORDB_URL`.
  - `tests/test_store_url.py` — 5 new URL-parser cases.
  - `tests/test_errors_format.py` — 3 new snapshot tests
    (`missing_optional_dependency__falkordb`,
    `invalid_argument_type__falkordb_target`,
    `invalid_store_url__falkordb_no_host`); rebaseline of
    `invalid_store_url__unsupported_scheme` to list the new scheme.
- **Docs**: `docs/reference/event-store-falkordb.md` (operator-facing
  reference); `mkdocs.yml` nav + snippet list wiring; `README.md`
  install section update; `CHANGELOG.md`; `v1.1-plan.md` Theme J entry.

## URL form

```
falkor://[user:pass@]host[:port]/<graph_name>
falkordb://...                                  # alias
```

Host is required; port defaults to `6379`; path is the FalkorDB graph
name (defaults to `activegraph` when omitted).

## Testing

- Full local suite passes: `611 passed, 18 skipped` (the 3 pre-existing
  failures — anthropic API-key check, wheel-completeness, mkdocs llms-txt
  — are unrelated to this PR; verified by stashing and re-running on
  `main`).
- FalkorDB conformance against `docker run -p 6379:6379 falkordb/falkordb:latest`:
  all 9 `EventStoreConformance` tests pass.
- `fork_run` smoke-tested end-to-end: 5 events parent → fork at `evt_2`
  → child has `[evt_0, evt_1, evt_2]`, lineage metadata correct,
  `list_runs` returns both.

```
$ ACTIVEGRAPH_TEST_FALKORDB_URL=falkor://localhost:6379/agtest \
    pytest tests/test_falkordb_store.py -v
...
9 passed
```

## Memory / Performance Impact

- Event log: one node per event + one edge per event + one node per
  run. Property storage is JSON-encoded `payload` (string) — matches
  Postgres `JSONB`-as-text round-trip semantics.
- `seq` allocation: read-modify-write of `r.next_seq` on the Run node
  inside one Cypher query. Atomic because FalkorDB serializes queries
  per graph — no explicit transaction needed.
- No impact on existing SQLite / Postgres / InMemory code paths.

## Deferred / Out of scope

- **Phase 2** — graph-projection backend (materialize the runtime
  graph itself into FalkorDB for external Cypher). Scoped in the
  module docstring and the v1.1 plan; requires a contract amendment
  on coupling (derivative-replay vs. live-write-through vs. opt-in-per-run).
- **Phase 3** — reuse FalkorDB's Cypher engine for the behavior-subscription
  Cypher subset. Future.
- **CI job** — the repo has no general unit-test CI workflow nor a
  Postgres CI counterpart to mirror; adding a FalkorDB-only opt-in job
  in isolation would be out of pattern. Run locally with the docker
  one-liner above. Filed for a future operator-tests CI workflow.

## Related Issues

User request: "how can we add FalkorDB support to this project?"
Plan filed at `v1.1-plan.md` Theme J → `STORE-FALKORDB`.

title: behavior runner: retry on llm.network_error before stubbing as empty
body:
When an @llm_behavior call fails with reason=llm.network_error (API credit-out, transient 5xx, connection reset), the runner currently stubs {"facts": []} and persists that to the event log. This makes credit-out indistinguishable from legitimate empty extractions and silently corrupts long-running caches.

Encountered during activegraph-longmemeval Post 3 cache build: ~31% of 38,000 entries were corrupted stubs from a mid-build credit exhaustion event. Recovery required dropping affected entries and re-extracting on resume. See https://activegraph.ai/blog/compile-from-the-log-dont-replace-it section 2.2.

Suggested fix: add N-retry with exponential backoff on llm.network_error (and other transient classes) before falling back to the empty-stub event. The empty-stub event should remain available as the terminal failure mode after retries exhaust.

title: Add support for FalkorDB graph store
body:
## Problem statement

Active Graph keeps the materialized graph — objects, relations, and patches —
in process memory (`InMemoryGraphStore`), rebuilt from the event log on every
run. That's the right default, but it leaves three things hard to do once a
run's current-state view gets interesting:

- **Query current state with a graph query language.** There's no way to ask
  "what does the graph look like right now?" with Cypher — dashboards, ad-hoc
  exploration, and graph-algorithm work all have to walk Python objects.
- **Share the projection across processes.** A live run and a separate
  read-only inspector (a dashboard, a sidecar) can't look at the same
  current-state view; each would rebuild its own in-memory copy.
- **Keep a large projection off the heap.** Projections that don't fit
  comfortably in process memory have nowhere else to go.

The event log already has a durable home behind the `EventStore` seam
(SQLite/Postgres). The *projection* has no equivalent seam — it's hardwired to
process memory. The goal is to make *where the current-state view is
materialized* a pluggable choice, without touching the "log is the source of
truth" model.

## Current workaround

There isn't a clean one. Today you'd have to manually export the projection
into your own store after a run and re-query it out of band — with no
read-through, so it drifts the moment anything mutates:

```python
rt.run_goal("…")

# Hand-roll an export into whatever external store you have.
for obj in rt.graph.all_objects():
    my_graph_db.upsert_node(obj.id, obj.type, obj.data)
for rel in rt.graph.all_relations():
    my_graph_db.upsert_edge(rel.id, rel.source, rel.target, rel.type)
```

This duplicates the projector logic, has to be re-run on every change, and
can't be used to inspect a recorded run (`Runtime.load` / `Runtime.fork`
always rebuild in memory). For larger graphs there's no workaround at all — the
projection must fit in the heap.

## Proposed solution

Introduce a `GraphStore` seam for the materialized projection, parallel to the
existing `EventStore` seam for the log, plus a FalkorDB-backed implementation.

Concretely:

- `GraphStore` abstraction with the current in-memory behavior as the default
  `InMemoryGraphStore`, and a `FalkorDBGraphStore` that backs the projection
  with a FalkorDB graph (objects/relations/patches as labelled nodes; all
  values passed as bound Cypher params).
- Two FalkorDB connection modes: a running server via the `falkordb` client
  (explicit `url=`/`host=` args **or** `FALKORDB_URL` / `FALKORDB_HOST`
  (`_PORT` / `_USERNAME` / `_PASSWORD`) env vars), falling back to the embedded
  `falkordblite` engine. Behind optional extras
  (`activegraph[falkordb]` / `activegraph[falkordb-embedded]`), kept out of
  `[all]`/`[dev]`.
- Wire the seam in at the library level only — `Graph(graph_store=…)`, and
  threaded through `Runtime.load(…, graph_store=…)` and
  `Runtime.fork(…, graph_store=…)` so recorded runs and forks can rematerialize
  in FalkorDB too. **No CLI flag**: the CLI's read commands operate on the log
  and are intentionally infrastructure-light, so the projection backend stays a
  programmatic choice.

```python
from activegraph import Graph, Runtime, FalkorDBGraphStore

store = FalkorDBGraphStore(host="localhost", port=6379, graph_name="run-42")
graph = Graph(graph_store=store)
rt = Runtime(graph=graph, behaviors=[...])
# … or replay an existing run into FalkorDB:
rt = Runtime.load("runs.db", run_id="run-42", graph_store=store)
```

Explicitly **out of scope**: the event log stays the source of truth. The
`GraphStore` is a disposable projection — durability and audit continue to come
from the `EventStore`, and a wiped FalkorDB graph is fully rebuilt by replaying
the log. This is additive and the in-memory default is unchanged.

title: FalkorDB relations-as-nodes break native traversal and visualization
body:
## Problem statement

`FalkorDBGraphStore` stores each relation as a standalone `AGRelation` *node*
carrying `source`/`target` id properties, rather than as a native graph edge.
That was a deliberate choice to preserve the in-memory store's
**dangling-relation** semantics (a relation may reference objects that don't
exist yet, which a native Cypher edge can't express), but it undermines the
main reason to back the projection with a graph database:

- **Visualization isn't graph-native.** In FalkorDB Browser the graph renders
  as a cloud of disconnected `AGObject` and `AGRelation` nodes with no edges
  between them. You can't *see* the graph.
- **Native traversal/algorithms don't apply.** Variable-length paths
  (`MATCH (a)-[*1..3]->(b)`), shortest-path, and graph algorithms operate on
  real relationships. With relations-as-nodes, every query manually joins
  `AGRelation.source`/`.target` back to `AGObject.id`; the guide currently has
  to tell users to match `AGRelation` nodes by their `source`/`target`
  properties and warns that edge-traversal algorithms don't apply directly.

The modeling round-trips correctly but defeats the value proposition (a
Cypher-queryable, shareable, *graph-native* current-state view). The goal is
for the FalkorDB projection to be a real graph — true edges between object
nodes — without losing dangling-relation support or cascade semantics.

## Current workaround

Query relations as nodes and join back to objects by hand:

```cypher
// "what does Alice know?" — no native traversal available today
MATCH (r:AGRelation {type: 'knows'})
MATCH (s:AGObject {id: r.source})
MATCH (t:AGObject {id: r.target})
WHERE s.data CONTAINS 'Alice'
RETURN t.id, t.data
```

Every relationship hop is a manual property-join. Multi-hop traversal,
shortest path, and any graph algorithm are effectively unavailable, and the
Browser view is unusable as a visualization. There is no client-side
workaround that yields a genuinely graph-native store — the modeling has to
change inside `FalkorDBGraphStore`.

## Proposed solution

Model relations as **native edges with a single fixed relationship type
`AGRelation`**, keeping the relation's `type` (plus `id`/`data`/`provenance`)
as **edge properties**:

```
(s)-[:AGRelation {id, type, data, provenance}]->(t)
```

Because the relationship type is a fixed literal, **every value stays a bound
`$param`** — no string interpolation, no injection surface, and no need to
escape or constrain relation `type` strings. The store becomes graph-native
(real edges, native traversal, a connected Browser view); traversal by kind is
a property filter: `MATCH (s)-[r:AGRelation {type:'knows'}]->(t)`.

### Node model: a shared `:AGNode` endpoint label

Dangling relations need an endpoint node to exist *before* its object does, so
decouple "is this object known?" from "does this node exist?". Every endpoint
carries a shared structural label `:AGNode`; real objects additionally carry
`:AGObject`:

- **Object** → `:AGNode:AGObject` (+ `type`/`version`/`data`/`provenance`)
- **Placeholder** (dangling endpoint) → `:AGNode` only

The shared `:AGNode` label is **required for correctness and performance**, not
cosmetics:

- A bare, label-less node can't be indexed (FalkorDB indexes are per-label), so
  `MERGE (s {id:$src})` in `put_relation` would have no index to probe and
  degrade to a **full node scan on every relation write**.
- MERGEing on a *type-specific* label instead (e.g. `:AGObject`) to get the
  index risks **duplicate-identity nodes** when the same id later promotes or
  already exists under different circumstances. The MERGE label has to be one
  that every endpoint shares — hence `:AGNode`.

**Placeholder state is derived, not labeled.** A dangling endpoint is exactly
`:AGNode AND NOT :AGObject`; there is no separate `:AGPlaceholder` label. This
keeps a single source of truth and avoids label churn — e.g. `remove_object`
on a still-referenced object naturally demotes it back to a placeholder (the
node survives because it still has edges) with no extra label bookkeeping. If
direct introspection of dangling endpoints is ever wanted, `:AGPlaceholder` is
a cheap additive follow-on.

```cypher
// find dangling endpoints, no extra label needed
MATCH (n:AGNode) WHERE NOT n:AGObject RETURN n.id
```

### Operation mapping (sketch)

| Op | Cypher |
|---|---|
| `put_object` | `MERGE (o:AGNode {id:$id}) SET o:AGObject, o.type=$type, o.version=$v, o.data=$data, o.provenance=$prov` |
| `put_relation` | `MERGE (s:AGNode {id:$src}) MERGE (t:AGNode {id:$tgt}) MERGE (s)-[r:AGRelation {id:$id}]->(t) SET r.type=$type, r.data=$data, r.provenance=$prov` |
| `all_objects` | `MATCH (o:AGObject) RETURN …` (placeholders excluded for free) |
| `get_relation` / `all_relations` | `MATCH (s)-[r:AGRelation]->(t) RETURN r.id, s.id, t.id, r.type, r.data, r.provenance` (`source`/`target` come from the endpoints) |
| `remove_object` | drop `:AGObject` + props; delete the node if it has no remaining edges, else leave it as a `:AGNode` placeholder |
| `remove_relation` | delete `r` by `r.id`, then delete either endpoint left as a bare `:AGNode` placeholder with no remaining edges |

`source`/`target` stop being stored properties — they fall out of the edge's
endpoints, which is the whole point.

### Indexes

FalkorDB supports both node- and relationship-property indexes:

```cypher
CREATE INDEX FOR (n:AGNode)        ON (n.id)     -- backs endpoint MERGE
CREATE INDEX FOR (n:AGObject)      ON (n.id)     -- backs object reads
CREATE INDEX FOR ()-[r:AGRelation]->() ON (r.id)    -- get/remove relation by id
CREATE INDEX FOR ()-[r:AGRelation]->() ON (r.type)  -- traversal by kind
CREATE INDEX FOR (n:AGPatch)       ON (n.id)
```

A node labeled `:AGNode:AGObject` is present in *both* label indexes, so
endpoint merges (`:AGNode`) and object reads (`:AGObject`) are each
index-backed.

### What this preserves

- **Dangling relations** — placeholder `:AGNode` endpoints stand in until the
  object arrives and promotes to `:AGObject`. ✅
- **Cascade-on-removal** — unchanged; the `core.graph` projector still deletes a
  removed object's relations, which now deletes edges. ✅
- **Round-trip fidelity** — `id`/`type`/`data`/`provenance` ride on the edge;
  `source`/`target` come from the endpoints. ✅
- **Security** — fixed relationship type means all values remain bound
  `$params`. ✅

### Other notes

- **No data migration.** The FalkorDB store is a disposable projection of the
  event log, so changing its on-disk shape migrates nothing — existing runs
  re-replay (`Runtime.load(..., graph_store=…)`) into the new layout. Low-risk
  by construction.
- **Conformance.** The change is invisible to `GraphStoreConformance` (same
  observable behavior); add cases for placeholder promotion (relation before
  object) and placeholder cleanup on relation removal.
- **Tradeoff (cosmetic).** All edges share the label `AGRelation`; the relation
  kind lives in the `type` property, so Browser styling/filtering keys off the
  property rather than the edge label. This is the price of keeping the write
  path injection-free, and it matches the `type`-as-attribute shape the current
  node modeling already uses.

This is a behavior-preserving internal remodeling of `FalkorDBGraphStore`
only; the `GraphStore` contract, the in-memory store, and the event log are
untouched.

title: feat(falkordb): implement native edges for relations
body:
resolves #41

## Summary

Remodels `FalkorDBGraphStore` so relations are stored as **native FalkorDB edges**
between object nodes instead of standalone `AGRelation` *nodes* with `source`/`target`
id properties. The projection becomes a real, traversable graph — connected in the
FalkorDB Browser and usable with native variable-length paths and graph algorithms —
without losing dangling-relation support or cascade semantics.

This is a behavior-preserving internal remodeling of `FalkorDBGraphStore` only. The
`GraphStore` contract, the in-memory store, and the event log are untouched, and
because the store is a disposable projection of the event log there is **no data
migration** — existing runs re-replay into the new layout.

## What changed

- **Relations are native edges with a single fixed relationship type.**
  `(s)-[:AGRelation {id, type, data, provenance}]->(t)`. The relation's `type`
  (plus `id`/`data`/`provenance`) rides on the edge as properties; `source`/`target`
  are no longer stored — they fall out of the endpoints, making the graph the single
  source of truth for connectivity. Traversal by kind is a property filter:
  `MATCH (s)-[r:AGRelation {type:'knows'}]->(t)`.
- **Shared `:AGNode` endpoint label.** Every endpoint carries a structural `:AGNode`
  label; real objects additionally carry `:AGObject`. `put_relation` MERGEs endpoints
  on `:AGNode` (index-backed, no full scans) and `put_object` promotes the same node
  in place with `SET o:AGObject`.
- **Dangling relations via derived placeholders.** A dangling endpoint is exactly
  `:AGNode AND NOT :AGObject` — placeholder-ness is derived, never a stored flag.
  When the object later arrives the node is promoted in place; when a relation is
  removed, any endpoint left as an orphaned placeholder (no remaining edges) is
  garbage-collected.
- **Cascade-on-removal unchanged.** The `core.graph` projector still deletes a removed
  object's relations (now edges), so behavior is identical across every `GraphStore`.
- **Indexes.** `AGNode(id)` (backs endpoint MERGE), `AGObject(id)` (object reads),
  relationship-property indexes `AGRelation(id)` and `AGRelation(type)`, and
  `AGPatch(id)`. A `:AGNode:AGObject` node appears in both label indexes.

## Security

Because the relationship type is a fixed literal (`AGRelation`), every value stays a
bound `$param` — no string interpolation and no injection surface, even for
user-supplied relation `type` strings.

## Tradeoff

All edges share the `AGRelation` label and the relation kind lives in the `type`
property, so Browser styling/filtering keys off the property rather than the edge
label. This is the price of keeping the write path injection-free and matches the
`type`-as-attribute shape the projection already uses.

## Testing

  object), placeholder cleanup on relation removal, and native-edge round-tripping;
  the existing `GraphStoreConformance` suite passes unchanged (same observable
  behavior).
- Live FalkorDB run (Docker container) green; persistence/fork/graph suites pass.

title: FalkorDB: structural Graph queries scan the whole projection instead of pushing down to Cypher
body:
## Problem

Every `Graph` query method evaluates its filter/traversal in Python by enumerating
the full materialized projection on each call:

- `Graph.objects(type=...)` / `query(...)` and `has_object_of_type(...)` iterate
  `all_objects()`
- `Graph.relations(...)` and `Graph.get_relations(...)` iterate `all_relations()`
- `Graph.neighborhood(...)` runs a Python BFS over `all_relations()`

For the in-memory backend this is cheap. For `FalkorDBGraphStore` it means every
narrow query fetches and JSON-decodes **every** object/relation in the projection
just to answer questions the database could answer directly — e.g. "objects of type
X", "relations from node Y", or a 1-hop neighborhood. This scales with the size of
the whole graph rather than the size of the result, so FalkorDB is currently only
practical for small projections and can't push traversals into the engine where it
has indexes and native edges.

## Expected

Structural queries (type filters, source/target/type relation lookups, and
neighborhood walks) should be evaluated close to the data — as Cypher inside FalkorDB
— returning only the matching rows. Results must remain **identical** to the current
Python behavior across all backends.

## Proposed approach

- Add optional query hooks to the `GraphStore` interface (`find_objects`,
  `find_relations`, `neighborhood`) with Python defaults that exactly reproduce
  today's behavior, so the base class stays the single source of truth for semantics
  and existing backends are unchanged.
- Have `Graph` delegate to those hooks.
- Override them with Cypher in `FalkorDBGraphStore` (including a native
  variable-length path query for `neighborhood`).
- Enforce parity with a conformance suite that runs the same assertions against every
  backend.

## Out of scope

- Pushing the rich `where` predicate down. Since `data` is stored as a JSON blob (not
  native, indexable properties), `where` should continue to evaluate in Python over
  the pushed-down subset. Native flattening/dual-write for `where` push-down is a
  separate future effort.
- `View` snapshots and whole-graph consumers (diffing, prompt building, pattern
  matching, registry, CLI status) that legitimately need the full projection.

title: perf(falkordb): push structural Graph queries down to Cypher
body:
fix #43 
depends on #42 

## Summary

`Graph` query methods previously evaluated every filter and traversal in Python
by scanning the full materialized projection (`all_objects()` / `all_relations()`)
on each call. For `FalkorDBGraphStore` that means fetching and JSON-decoding every
entity even to answer a narrow query (e.g. "objects of type X" or a 1-hop
neighborhood). This PR lets backends evaluate structural queries close to the data
while keeping query semantics identical across all backends.

## What changed

- **New optional query hooks on the `GraphStore` ABC** — `find_objects`,
  `find_relations`, and `neighborhood` — with working Python defaults computed over
  `all_objects` / `all_relations`. The base class is the canonical definition of
  their semantics; `InMemoryGraphStore` inherits them unchanged.
- **`Graph` delegates to the hooks** instead of scanning:
  - `Graph.objects(type=...)` / `query(...)` and `has_object_of_type(...)` →
    `find_objects`
  - `Graph.relations(...)` and `Graph.get_relations(...)` → `find_relations`
  - `Graph.neighborhood(...)` → `neighborhood`
- **`FalkorDBGraphStore` overrides the hooks with Cypher** so type filters, relation
  lookups, and neighborhood walks run inside the database (the neighborhood walk uses
  a native variable-length path over `AGRelation` edges) and return only matching
  rows instead of the whole projection.
- **`where` predicates still run in Python.** `Graph.objects(where=...)` pushes the
  *type* filter down but applies the `where` clause in Python over the returned
  subset, because the structured `data` payload is stored as a JSON string rather
  than as native, indexable properties.

## Scope / non-goals

- `View` (frozen snapshot) and whole-graph consumers (diffing, prompt building,
  pattern matching, the registry, CLI status) legitimately read the full projection
  and are intentionally left unchanged.
- Pushing `where` predicates down (would require flattening selected scalar fields to
  native properties + dual-write) is deferred to a future change.

## Correctness & parity

- Backward-compatible quirks preserved: `get_relations` keeps the v0 behavior of
  ignoring `object_id` for an unrecognized `direction`, and the `"both"`
  source-OR-target membership test (which the AND-only `find_relations` can't express)
  stays in `Graph`.
- New parity tests in `GraphStoreConformance` run the **same** assertions against
  both `InMemoryGraphStore` (the reference) and `FalkorDBGraphStore`, covering:
  `find_objects` (none + type filter), `find_relations` (all source/target/type
  combinations, including dangling endpoints), and `neighborhood` (depth 0/1/2/3, a
  placeholder midpoint, a cycle, and non-object/unknown starts).

## Security

Every value crosses the Cypher boundary as a bound `$param`. The only literal spliced
into a query is the variable-length upper bound `*1..{hops}`, where `hops = int(depth)`
is a caller-owned coerced integer — no user text, no injection surface.

## Testing

- InMemory conformance suite: green (includes the new parity tests).
- Live FalkorDB suite (Docker container): 22 passed, including the variable-length
  path queries.
- Doc-link, `llms.txt`, `Graph`, and `GraphStore` suites pass; docstring gate passes.

## Docs / changelog

- Updated the "How entities are stored" notes in `docs/guides/using-falkordb.md` to
  describe push-down vs. the Python-evaluated `where`.
- Added an `[Unreleased]` entry to `CHANGELOG.md`.

title: FalkorDB: Push structural graph reads down to the GraphStore so large FalkorDB-backed graphs query inside the database
body:
### Problem

`FalkorDBGraphStore` lets the materialized projection live in FalkorDB, but the read paths that matter on a large graph still ran in Python over the *whole* projection:

- **Pattern matching** walked the chain hop-by-hop, issuing an N+1 of per-hop queries and scanning every candidate object/relation on each event. On FalkorDB this dragged the entire object/edge set out of the database and JSON-decoded it per event.
- **Type-scoped behavior views** (`include_types`) and **relation-behavior matching** materialized every object/edge and filtered in Python.
- **Cascade delete** on `object.removed` scanned every relation to find the few touching the removed node.

The result: cost scaled with **graph size**, not **result size**. A 2-hop pattern match over 20k objects took ~8.9 s — most of it pulling and decoding rows that don't match.

### Proposal

Add a small set of **optional query hooks** to the `GraphStore` interface that a backend MAY override to push the filter/traversal into the database, with the base class providing a Python default that is the single source of truth for semantics:

- `match_chain(node_types, rels)` — resolve a linear node→rel→node chain (the engine behind pattern matching). FalkorDB resolves the whole chain in one index-backed Cypher query.
- `find_objects_in_types(types)` — OR-of-types read (`type IN [...]`) used by type-scoped views.
- Route relation-behavior matching and cascade delete through the already-pushed-down `find_relations(...)` hook.

Keep the parts that can't be translated faithfully (the `where` predicate language, node `{prop: value}` equality over the JSON `data` blob, variable-consistency) in Python, evaluated over the pushed-down candidate set — so query semantics stay **byte-for-byte identical** across every backend.

title: perf(falkordb): push structural reads down to the GraphStore
body:
resolves #45
depends on #44 

### What

Collapse the pattern matcher's per-hop N+1 queries and several whole-projection scans into pushed-down `GraphStore` hooks, so large-graph work runs inside the database on FalkorDB while staying identical on the in-memory default.

### Changes

- **`match_chain` hook** — resolves a linear `node → rel → node` chain. The base-class default mirrors the matcher's homomorphic depth-first walk; `FalkorDBGraphStore` resolves the entire chain in **one** index-backed Cypher query instead of one round-trip per hop per candidate. The pattern matcher now routes through it, applying node `{prop: value}` equality, variable-consistency, and `WHERE` in Python over the resolved chains.
- **`find_objects_in_types` hook** — OR-of-types read (single `type IN [...]` query on FalkorDB). The view builder uses it for type-scoped views (`include_types` without an `around` anchor); the default single-pass scan preserves order so the in-memory `View` is unchanged.
- **Relation-behavior matching** filters candidate edges via `relations(type=...)` instead of scanning every edge per event.
- **Cascade delete** on `object.removed` uses two scoped `find_relations` lookups (out + in edges, deduped) instead of a full edge scan.
- Every value still crosses the Cypher boundary as a bound `$param`; only generated names and the closed `{right,left}` direction set are spliced — no injection surface.

### Semantics & safety

The rich `where` language stays in `Graph`, evaluated in Python — only structural filters (types, directions) push down. The base `GraphStore` is the single source of truth for each hook's semantics, and a **differential test suite** builds the same graph on both backends and asserts identical `match_chain` / `find_objects_in_types` / view / relation-behavior results, so backends can't drift.

### Performance

New benchmark_falkordb.py and a "Performance" section in the FalkorDB guide document the trade-offs (indicative, hardware-dependent). Headline at 20k objects:

| Operation | InMemory | FalkorDB |
|---|---|---|
| 2-hop pattern match | 8,920 ms | **300 ms** (~30× faster) |
| neighborhood depth=2 | 1.07 ms | 0.94 ms |
| full scan / writes | faster | slower (round-trip + JSON) |

In-memory wins raw latency on small/medium graphs and always on writes; the pushed-down structural reads flip the comparison at scale because their cost tracks **result** size, not graph size. Documented as a **latency win, not a token win** — both backends produce an identical `View`, so prompt tokens are unchanged.

### Tests

- `GraphStoreConformance` gains `find_objects_in_types` and `match_chain` cases (run on both backends).
- `test_falkordb_store` adds FalkorDB-gated differential InMemory-vs-FalkorDB tests for `match_chain`, `find_objects_in_types`, the view-builder `include_types` path, and relation-behavior matching.
- Full default suite green; combined FalkorDB-gated run green; doc and docstring gates green.

## Summary

This PR adds machine-readable agent-discovery files to the documentation site root to improve AI agent and coding assistant discoverability. It introduces a post-build hook that mirrors `/llms.txt` to `/llms.md` for agents probing well-known markdown paths, and adds a `/robots.txt` file pointing crawlers to the sitemap and agent-discovery entry points.

## Key Changes

- **New post-build hook** (`scripts/mkdocs_hooks.py`): Copies the generated `llms.txt` to `llms.md` at the site root after the mkdocs build completes. This serves agents that probe well-known markdown root paths (e.g., `/llms.md`, `/agents.md`) on static hosts that cannot perform Accept-header content negotiation.

- **New robots.txt** (`docs/robots.txt`): Static file copied verbatim by mkdocs to the site root. Declares a wildcard User-agent block and points to the canonical sitemap URL at `https://docs.activegraph.ai/sitemap.xml`. Includes comments documenting the machine-readable entry points.

- **MkDocs configuration** (`mkdocs.yml`): Registered the new post-build hook in the `hooks:` block with explanatory comments about the cold-discovery path for AI agents.

- **Test coverage** (`tests/test_llms_txt.py`): Added two new slow-marked tests:
  - `test_llms_md_mirrors_llms_txt`: Asserts `/llms.md` exists and is a byte-for-byte mirror of `/llms.txt`
  - `test_robots_txt_present_and_points_at_sitemap`: Verifies `/robots.txt` exists, declares a wildcard User-agent, and contains the canonical sitemap pointer

- **Documentation updates**:
  - Updated `docs/index.md` with a new "Machine-readable docs" section describing the three agent-discovery entry points
  - Updated `CHANGELOG.md` with details about the new agent-discovery files and PyPI metadata improvements
  - Updated `tests/test_doc_links.py` to include `/llms.md` in the build-generated URLs set

- **PyPI metadata** (`pyproject.toml`): Added project URLs (`Documentation`, `Repository`, `Changelog`, `Issues`) to help tooling and AI agents verify this is the official package for docs.activegraph.ai.

- **CI/CD** (`.github/workflows/docs.yml`): Added `scripts/mkdocs_hooks.py` to the paths that trigger the docs workflow.

## Implementation Details

The `/llms.md` mirror solves a static-host limitation: GitHub Pages serves `.md` files with `Content-Type: text/markdown` but cannot negotiate content types based on Accept headers on the homepage. By providing an exact byte-for-byte copy of the already-markdown `llms.txt` as `llms.md`, agents arriving cold (from web search, without reading llms.txt first) can discover and ingest the documentation via well-known markdown paths.

The post-build hook fails loudly if `llms.txt` is missing rather than silently shipping an incomplete site, catching configuration errors early. The test suite gates both files with byte-equality and presence assertions.

title: FalkorDB: design pass for `where` predicate push-down (property flattening / dual-write)
body:
## Problem

`where` predicates are the one read surface that still always evaluates in Python. The v1.2 query hooks (#43/#45) pushed structural filters — type scans, relation lookups, neighborhoods, whole pattern chains — down into FalkorDB, so their cost now scales with result size. But `Graph.objects(where=...)`, `View` object filters, and pattern `WHERE` clauses evaluate over the pushed-down candidate set in Python, because the structured payload is stored as a single JSON `data` property on the node. Cypher can't index or compare into it, so a query like

```python
graph.objects(type="claim", where={"confidence": {">": 0.8}})
```

pushes `type="claim"` down but then fetches and JSON-decodes **every** claim to keep the few above 0.8. On a projection with many objects of the filtered type, cost scales with the *type population*, not the result — the same shape of gap #43 closed for structural queries.

This was deliberately scoped out twice: #43's out-of-scope note named "native flattening/dual-write for `where` push-down" as a separate future effort, and CONTRACT v1.2 #4 locked the split rule (structural filters push down; the `where` language stays in Python) while naming this design pass as the follow-on. This issue is that follow-on. Because it deliberately revisits a locked rule, it is **design-first**: no implementation lands before the questions below are answered and locked in a CONTRACT amendment.

## Current workaround

Narrow the candidate set with what already pushes down (`type=`, `objects_in_types`, relation scoping, pattern chains) and accept the Python filter over the remainder. This is correct and often fine — the v1.2 hooks mean the Python side only sees candidates, not the whole graph — but it leaves indexable comparisons (`confidence > 0.8`, `status == "open"`) unindexed on exactly the backend adopters chose for scale.

## Proposed approach (the design questions to answer)

**1. Which subset of the `where` language translates faithfully?**
The language is small: dotted paths, bare literals meaning equality, and `{op: value}` with ops `> < >= <= == != in / not in` (plus, in pattern `WHERE`, `AND` / `NOT` / `NOT EXISTS` composition). A faithful translation must preserve some deliberately Python-flavored semantics:

- missing path ⇒ `None`, and ordered comparisons on `None` are `False` (Cypher's `NULL` propagation happens to align, but needs conformance coverage, not assumption);
- `in` / `not in` are Python membership over strings *and* lists — Cypher `IN` doesn't do substring matching, so string-membership either translates to `CONTAINS` (strings only) or stays in Python;
- equality across JSON types (numbers vs strings, nested dicts/lists) must match Python `==` exactly — nested dict/list equality likely stays in Python.

The plausible v1-subset: top-level scalar fields with `== != > < >= <=` and list-membership `in`. Everything outside the subset stays in Python over the pushed-down remainder — partial push-down (translate what translates, post-filter the rest) rather than all-or-nothing.

**2. Opt-in per-type vs global flattening?** Flattening writes `data` keys as native node properties so Cypher can index and compare them. Global flattening is simple but pays write cost and property-key sprawl for every type, including ones nobody filters; per-type opt-in (e.g. the pack's `ObjectType` declaring indexable fields, or a store-level `flatten={"claim": ["confidence", "status"]}`) keeps cost where the value is, at the price of a config surface and asymmetric query plans. Leaning per-type opt-in, but this is exactly the decision the amendment must lock.

**3. What does dual-write cost, and who pays it?** Flattened properties are a second copy of (part of) `data`: every `object.created` / `patch.applied` write updates both. Costs to quantify in the design pass: write amplification per event, property-count limits and index maintenance in FalkorDB, collision rules when a `data` key shadows a structural property (`id`, `type` are reserved), and re-flattening on config change. The projection being disposable (CONTRACT v1.2 #1) is the escape hatch: changing the flattening config never migrates data — re-replay the log into the new shape, same as the v1.2 #3 layout change.

**4. What does `GraphStoreConformance` assert?** The v1.2 #4/#5 rule stands: Python defaults define semantics; a backend override MUST return identical results. The suite would grow a `where`-parity section: for each operator × (present / missing / `None`-valued / type-mismatched path) × (flattened / unflattened type), the pushed-down result set equals the Python evaluator's, byte for byte. The subset boundary is also asserted: predicates outside the translatable subset must still be answered correctly (via the post-filter path), never silently dropped.

## Out of scope

- Any implementation before the four answers above are locked in a CONTRACT amendment (the v1.2 #4 split rule is being deliberately revisited, so it needs its own amendment, not a silent in-PR change).
- Pattern-`WHERE` composition (`AND` / `NOT` / `NOT EXISTS`) push-down — the object-query subset comes first; pattern `WHERE` inherits whatever subset is locked.
- Other backends. The design should be expressible through `GraphStore` hooks so Neo4j/Postgres-graph backends (CONTRACT v1.2 #5) can adopt it, but FalkorDB is the reference implementation.
- Changing the in-memory default's behavior in any way.

---

*Provenance: @dudizimber drove the v1.2 GraphStore arc end-to-end (#38/#41/#43/#45 → PRs #39/#46); this is that arc's named follow-on (CONTRACT v1.2 #4). Filed in the same problem → workaround → approach → out-of-scope shape as that series.*

**Fix 1 — child stderr was discarded.** The child was spawned `stderr=subprocess.DEVNULL`, so any crash before it could write its report tail (module-import failure, rlimit setup, anything pre-`main`) surfaced as an opaque `crashed` / "exited N with no report tail" and the real exception was gone. stderr is now PIPED and, on a crashed/no-tail exit, its tail is folded into `TrialReport.detail`. **Fix 2 — the env allow-list broke legitimate environments (the design call).** The allow-list (`PATH`/`HOME`/`LANG` + `env_passthrough`) is a security control and correctly strips ambient platform vars — but on Replit/Nix, `REPLIT_PYTHONPATH` is how packages become importable, so the stripped child couldn't `import activegraph` at all. Code locations are not secrets, so a computed `PYTHONPATH` widens nothing the allow-list protects. The child imports the same code the parent can on any box, without the allow-list growing an entry. New `sandbox.preflight()` spawns a null-job child to verify startup end-to-end and raises `SandboxStartupError` with the cause if a child can't start — consumers fail loud at boot instead of opaque on the first trial.

Tests reproduce the restricted env faithfully via `-S` (skip `site.py`, exactly the "site-packages not on default path" shape): bare env fails with `ModuleNotFoundError`, the computed channel rescues it, and a planted secret provably does not cross the boundary.

title: Release v1.7.1 — portable macOS trial-child resource limits
body:
## What this releases

A macOS trial-child fix surfaced by a second soak — a macOS/arm64 box went RED on rotation 1, **exposed because** 1.7.0's import fix let the child finally reach `_apply_rlimits`. Additive, in `activegraph.sandbox`; packs pinned `>=1.6,<2.0` (and `>=1.5,<2.0`) keep working unchanged.

### Fix 1 — RLIMIT_AS portability (the crash)

`max_rss_bytes` maps to `RLIMIT_AS`, which is enforced on Linux but **rejected by the Darwin kernel** (`ValueError: current limit exceeds maximum limit` — Darwin does not support address-space limiting), so every limits-carrying trial crashed deterministically at `_child.py:58`.

Resource-limit application is now portable: an unsettable cap **degrades** rather than crashing or silently skipping. The child records a loud warning that surfaces in `TrialReport.warnings` and `.detail` and is logged; the wall-clock kill and event budget remain the active nets. Limit application never raises a hard limit (the target is clamped to the existing hard limit — that raise was the Darwin crash).

**The memory budget's guarantee is now stated per-platform:** enforced on Linux; announced-unavailable on macOS/Windows, where wall-clock + events bound the runaway-memory accident class. There is no honest Darwin substitute — `RLIMIT_RSS`/`RLIMIT_DATA` are unenforced against total address space, and a Python RSS watchdog is the OS-control imitation the design refuses. A BabyAGI author on macOS gets a memory net that **says it's off** rather than one that pretends to be on.

### Fix 2 — preflight must exercise limits (the false green — the real safety gap)

The 1.7.0 `preflight()` sent a null job with **no limits block**, so it never reached `_apply_rlimits` and passed on a box where every real trial then crashed. It now applies a representative limits block, catching the `RLIMIT_AS` class at the gate: on macOS it **passes with a memory-net warning** (returned + logged) rather than pass-then-crash; on a box that cannot start a child it still **raises** `SandboxStartupError` with the cause. `preflight()` now returns the degradation warnings (empty tuple = fully clean).

### Fix 3 — the 1.7.0 stderr capture

No change; confirming it earned its keep. The macOS digest surfaced the exact `RLIMIT_AS ValueError` verbatim, which is how this was diagnosed in one shot.

## Tests

The macOS crash can't regress: Linux applies clean, a **simulated Darwin rejection** (monkeypatched `setrlimit`) degrades without crashing, the target never exceeds the hard limit, preflight exercises the limit path, and the parent surfaces warnings into `TrialReport`. The remaining runtime hardening plan had three concrete gaps: embedding/provider I/O and result-affecting clocks were not fully replayable, trial execution was hardcoded to one module-level subprocess function, and local gate bypasses had no mandatory audit record. title: Avoid materializing FalkorDB payloads in has_object_of_type()
body:
## Problem statement

`Graph.has_object_of_type(type_)` currently evaluates `bool(self._state.find_objects(type_))`. With `FalkorDBGraphStore`, this reads every matching object's id, type, version, data, and provenance, then JSON-decodes both payload columns before discarding the objects and returning a boolean.

This is the remaining existence-check case from the query-pushdown work discussed in #43 and merged through #44/#46. I did not find an open issue or PR for a dedicated existence query.

Using embedded FalkorDB 0.10.0 with 20,000 objects split evenly across four types, one `claim` lookup with 5,000 matches performs 10,000 `json.loads` calls. The current materializing path measured 54.48 ms median over seven alternating samples; a bound scalar feasibility query performed no payload decodes and measured 0.513 ms median. Absolute timings are hardware-dependent, while the decode count is deterministic.

## Current workaround

Call `find_objects(type_)` and convert the returned list to `bool`. This preserves the existing semantics but materializes every matching object. Applications can issue backend-specific Cypher directly, but that bypasses the `Graph` and `GraphStore` interfaces.

## Proposed solution

1. Add a non-abstract `GraphStore.has_object_of_type(type_)` default that keeps `bool(find_objects(type_))` as the canonical behavior for third-party stores, including the existing runtime behavior where `None` means “any object.”
2. Delegate `Graph.has_object_of_type()` to that hook.
3. Override it in FalkorDB with one bound scalar `LIMIT 1` query that returns at most one row and no payload columns.
4. Add `AGObject(type)` to the existing index setup. `PROFILE` showed a label scan without it, including a full scan for an absent type; creating the index before population changed the plan to `Node By Index Scan` and reduced the 20,000-object absent median from about 3.46 ms to 0.50 ms.
5. Preserve empty-string types with a bound scalar label-scan fallback. In the reproduced embedded FalkorDB 0.10.0 setup, the range index did not retain empty strings, while the label-scan fallback found them.

A local candidate produces zero payload decodes and measures 0.480 ms median versus a 49.56 ms materializing reference (`103.3x` in that alternating run). Present, absent, empty-string, multiple-match, add, and remove-last cases match `InMemoryGraphStore`; the read emits no events or writes.

## Open questions

CONTRACT v1.2 #4 locks the current query-hook list. Would you accept an appended amendment that:

- adds `has_object_of_type` to that list;
- keeps the base Python default as the semantic source of truth;
- requires backend overrides to be conformance-equivalent;
- keeps the hook optional to override and non-abstract for existing third-party stores; and
- adds these existence cases to `GraphStoreConformance`?

Is the additional `AGObject(type)` index acceptable as part of the same focused change? If this shape is approved, I can open the implementation and test PR. I will not open it before agreement because it extends the locked GraphStore surface.

title: Caller mutation after Graph.emit() changes the in-memory event log but not SQLite
body:
## Reproduction

```python
from tempfile import TemporaryDirectory

from activegraph import Event, Graph, SQLiteEventStore


with TemporaryDirectory() as temp_dir:
    store = SQLiteEventStore(
        f"{temp_dir}/events.sqlite",
        run_id="run_mutability_repro",
    )
    graph = Graph()
    graph.attach_store(store)

    payload = {"nested": {"value": 1}}
    event = Event(
        id="evt_mutability_repro",
        type="custom.fact",
        payload=payload,
    )
    accepted = graph.emit(event)

    payload["nested"]["value"] = 2
    persisted = store.get_event(event.id)

    print("same_object_returned:", accepted is event)
    print("in_memory_value:", graph.events[0].payload["nested"]["value"])
    print("persisted_value:", persisted.payload["nested"]["value"])
```

Output:

```text
same_object_returned: True
in_memory_value: 2
persisted_value: 1
```

## Expected behavior

Once `Graph.emit()` accepts an event, later mutation of the caller-owned payload should not change the accepted event in the in-memory log. The in-memory and persisted representations should continue to describe the same accepted fact.

I would expect both values to remain `1`. This does not assume whether the implementation should copy the event, freeze payload data, or use another boundary.

## Actual behavior

`Graph.emit()` appends and returns the caller's original `Event`. The dataclass is frozen, but its nested payload remains mutable. Changing the original payload after acceptance changes `graph.events[0]` to `2`, while SQLite retains the `1` serialized during append.

No exception or warning is raised.

## Framework version

```text
activegraph 1.10.0
```

## Python version

Reproduced with:

```text
Python 3.12.3
Python 3.12.13
```

## OS

Reproduced in three clean Linux environments, including Ubuntu 24.04 and the current `python:3.12-slim` container image.

## Anything else worth knowing

The published `activegraph==1.10.0` package reproduced this in three independent clean installations, rather than an editable source checkout.

This appears to conflict with CONTRACT sections 2 and 3, which make the event log the source of truth and state that events are append-only and never edited. `activegraph/core/event.py` also describes events as never modified after `emit()`, while noting that the payload dictionary is not deeply frozen.
